notes: Brackets: Publication 106 PDF pages 6-7 print 2025 Tax Rate Schedules A ('For Single Taxpayers or Head of Household'), B (married filing jointly) and C (married filing separately). Head of household has no schedule of its own, so no head_of_household list is given (it uses single). The Form 1 Instructions Tax Table (PDF pages 38-43, taxable income under 100,000) was checked against the schedules at every row midpoint: 3,006 cells, none off by more than 1 dollar (the page 38 example, joint taxable income 28,653, prints 1,084; the schedule gives 1,084.38). The Tax Computation Worksheet (page 44) constants are the schedule's own arithmetic (single 5.3% minus 586.44 and 7.65% minus 8,183.76; joint 5.3% minus 781.92 and 7.65% minus 10,911.83; separate 7.65% minus 5,455.92 at 215,530 or over).
Publication 106 page 7: nonresidents and part-year residents prorate the income levels of the rates by Wisconsin income over federal AGI. This record is for full-year residents.

Filing status: Form 1 Instructions PDF page 13: 'If you file your federal return as a qualifying surviving spouse, you may file your Wisconsin return as head of household.' Wisconsin has no qualifying surviving spouse status of its own.

Standard deduction: Form 1 Instructions PDF pages 35-37 print only a table by line 7 Wisconsin income, in rows 'At least / But less than' 500 dollars wide (the first row 0 to 13,390, then 13,390 to 13,500, the last 155,000 to 155,169, then '155,169 or more' 0). No formula, rate or threshold is printed. The record holds the whole table as phase_out steps (every row where an amount changes; every figure printed). Judgement, derived and not printed: the rows are matched to the dollar at their midpoints by: single 13,560 less 12% of income over 19,550; married filing jointly 25,110 less 19.778% over 28,210; married filing separately 11,930 less 19.778% over 13,390; head of household 17,520 less 22.515% over 19,550 but never below the single amount (equal from the 57,000 row, 9,036). Single and head of household reach 0 at the 132,500 row, separate at 73,500; joint is 17 in the 155,000 row. A consumer using the steps gets the form's exact amount; the formula behind the table is not in the sources.

Standard deduction for a person who can be claimed as a dependent (Form 1 Instructions PDF page 15 worksheet): the smaller of the table amount and earned income plus 450 (at least 1,350). A short-period return or a federal Form 4563 exclusion gets no standard deduction (0).

Exemptions (Form 1 Instructions PDF pages 15-16, Form 1 line 10): 700 each for you and your spouse (0 for a person who can be claimed as a dependent), and 700 for each dependent listed on federal Form 1040; 250 more for you and for your spouse if 65 or older on December 31, 2025, only for a person allowed the 700 exemption. The booklets print no blind exemption or blind standard deduction, and no income limit on exemptions.

Social Security: Schedule SB line 4 subtracts the taxable benefits from federal Form 1040 line 6b, 'Social security benefits are not taxable for Wisconsin' (Schedule SB Instructions PDF page 2); Publication 126 PDF page 5, Publication 106 PDF page 4 and the FAQ say the same.

Pensions in general: Publication 126 PDF page 4 section 3: 'The amount of your retirement benefits that are taxable for federal income tax purposes are also taxable for Wisconsin. This is true even though the retirement benefit may be due to services performed in another state.' Example 1 there: an Illinois teacher's pension received by a full-year Wisconsin resident is taxable as on the federal return. Example 2: an IRA set up in Florida is taxable too.

Government pensions of other states (New York State included): no rule in the sources names any other state's pension or any reciprocity, and nothing treats them differently from Wisconsin's own post-1963 government pensions: they are taxable as on the federal return (Publication 126 page 4), and they are 'qualifying retirement income' for the two general subtractions (lines 16 and 17), so public_pension_other_state is in covers on those entries. 'New York' does not appear in the sources.

Judgement: lines 16 and 17 take 'retirement income from a qualified retirement plan or individual retirement account (IRA)'. Publication 126 PDF page 11 (section J) lists what a 'qualified retirement plan' includes: 401(a) trusts, SEPs, 403(a) and 403(b) annuities, IRAs, 457 plans of state and local governments, 'A government plan under sec. 414(d), IRC', and 501(c)(18) trusts. The FAQ ('Does Wisconsin have any general exclusion of retirement income?') says the two subtractions may be claimed 'for benefits other than those listed in Answer 1' (the exempt pre-1964 systems, military and railroad), and its example says exempt military pay may not also be claimed, which assumes government benefits are otherwise eligible. So public_pension and public_pension_other_state are in covers. The section J list is printed for nonresidents; the general-subtraction text does not repeat it.

Judgement: annuity is in covers on lines 16 and 17 only as annuity income from a qualified retirement plan (the line 17 worksheet line 2: 'Taxable pension and annuity income from a qualified retirement plan included on line 5b'). The sources do not say that an annuity bought outside a qualified plan or IRA qualifies.

Roth conversions: no source says whether a conversion counts for lines 16 or 17; roth_conversion is in covers_unclear. The line 17 worksheet line 1 takes 'Taxable IRA distributions from line 4b of your federal Form 1040', which is where a conversion is reported federally, but the booklet never names conversions.

Line 16 (24,000/48,000, 'Credits Restricted', first available for 2025, 2025 Wis. Act 15): Schedule SB Instructions PDF page 7: 'Individuals may subtract up to $24,000 of retirement income received. A married couple who file a joint return and are both as least 67 years old as of December 31, 2025, may subtract up to $48,000 of retirement income, regardless of how much retirement income each spouse received.' Recorded as two entries: the individual amount (each person 67 or older, up to 24,000 of that person's own qualifying income) and the joint amount (both spouses 67 or older, up to 48,000 of either spouse's). Judgement: a joint return with only one spouse 67 or older gets the individual amount, 24,000, of that spouse's own income: the 48,000 is printed only for 'both', and 'regardless of how much retirement income each spouse received' is said only of the pooled joint amount. Publication 106 page 4 ('you (or your spouse if married filing joint return)') states eligibility, the same words line 17 uses before a per-spouse worksheet.

Line 16 forfeits credits: Schedule SB Instructions PDF page 7 Caution and Publication 126 PDF page 8: no credit on Schedule CR or Form 1 lines 13-20 and 30-35 for the year, including carryforwards. Those lines are the itemized deduction credit (13), additional child and dependent care credit (14), blind worker transportation credit (15), school property tax credit (16, at most 300, 150 married separate or married head of household), working families credit (17, 'Do not enter any amount on this line'), married couple credit (18, at most 480), Schedule CR nonrefundable credits (19), credit for net tax paid to another state (20), earned income credit (30), farmland preservation (31), repayment credit (32), homestead credit (33), veterans property tax credit (34) and Schedule CR refundable credits (35). The schema has no field for a relief that bars credits; it is in who.other_conditions of both line 16 entries. The filer chooses: claim line 16 and lose the credits, or skip it.

Lines 16 and 17 stack: the line 17 worksheet (Schedule SB Instructions PDF page 8) line 4 removes 'the total amount subtracted on lines 12, 13, 14, 15, and 16' before the 5,000 limit, so both may be claimed, line 17 on what line 16 leaves. Neither has cannot_combine_with.

Line 17 (5,000, 'Income Restricted'): age 65 or older on December 31, 2025; federal AGI (Form 1 line 3) less than 15,000 single or head of household, 30,000 married filing jointly; married filing separately, the sum of both spouses' federal AGI less than 30,000 (Publication 126 page 8). Each spouse figured separately in the worksheet columns, so up to 10,000 on a joint return. 'Less than' is recorded as effect removes, applies_when at_or_over. Line 17 does not restrict credits.

Wisconsin's own and federal government pensions: taxable as federally (Publication 106 page 4 section 3.B), except payments from the seven listed pre-1964 local and state systems and the federal Civil Service Retirement System on a pre-1964 account (Schedule SB lines 13 and 14), and U.S. military, Coast Guard, NOAA and Public Health Service retirement pay (line 12). The Wisconsin Retirement System is not on the list (Publication 126 page 7 Example 1: the WRS part of an annuity is taxable). Thrift Savings Plan payments are taxable. No contributory-plan test is printed.

Lump-sum distributions reported on federal Form 4972 are added to Wisconsin income as ordinary income (Publication 126 page 5; Schedule AD line 6). Penalties: 33% of the federal penalty tax on IRAs and retirement plans (Form 1 line 25 'x .33'; Publication 126 page 13), not on an exempt pre-1964 system distribution. No field holds either.

Credits are not recorded as reliefs (design non-goal): itemized deduction credit 5% of certain federal itemized deductions over the Wisconsin standard deduction (Form 1 Schedule 1); married couple credit 3% of the smaller spouse's qualified earned income up to 16,000, at most 480 (Form 1 Schedule 2); school property tax credit; homestead credit (household income below 24,680, Publication 106 page 5).

Also not recorded as reliefs: medical care insurance and long-term care insurance subtractions (Schedule SB lines 6-7); unemployment compensation worksheet (line 3); 'Annuities that began after July 1, 1986, and before January 1, 1987' (Publication 126 page 9, a Schedule I adjustment); nonresident rules for retirement distributions (Publication 126 pages 11-12).

Capital gains: Schedule SB Instructions PDF page 2 line 5 names the 30% long-term capital gain exclusion (60% for farm assets), figured on Schedule WD; Schedule WD and its holding-period and loss rules are not in the sources. A capital gain distribution that is the only gain, with no Wisconsin loss carryover, takes 30% on line 5 directly.

Municipal interest: Schedule AD Instructions PDF pages 1-2, line 1: add 'interest you received from state, municipal, and other bonds', 'generally ... the amount shown as tax-exempt interest on line 2a of your federal Form 1040', which includes Wisconsin's own municipal bonds, except 18 listed kinds exempt for both federal and Wisconsin purposes (mostly bonds of named Wisconsin authorities and districts, bonds of Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, the Northern Mariana Islands and, if issued after October 16, 2004, American Samoa, and certain pre-1987 out-of-state public housing agency bonds), whether held directly or through a mutual fund. Recorded as 'other'.

U.S. government interest is subtracted on Schedule SB line 2 (not Ginnie Mae and similar 'guaranteed' securities), and the part of an IRA, Keogh or qualified deferred compensation distribution attributable to U.S. government securities interest is exempt (Publication 126 page 10 worksheet).
Indexing: no source says whether any figure is adjusted for inflation (searched index, inflation, adjusted annually).
No recapture: the Tax Computation Worksheet reproduces the schedules' own arithmetic.
